title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets, and Webhooks
summary: Compare the main API styles, see what each one looks like on the wire, and learn when to pick each one.
intro: Not every API works the same way. A shop's public API, the calls between a company's own services, a live chat, and a payment company telling your server that a card went through each fit a different style, and picking the wrong one costs speed, money, or months of work. This lesson walks through the styles you'll meet: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, the ways to push live updates (polling, server-sent events, and WebSockets), and webhooks. For each one, you'll see what it looks like on the wire, what it's good at, and what it costs. The last part helps you choose, and shows the three that Roombook uses.

steps.title: REST over HTTP
steps.body:
REST is the style most public APIs use, and the one this course builds. Its rules are the reason Roombook's addresses look the way they do, so they're worth knowing by name.

## Resources, methods, and representations

**REST**, short for Representational State Transfer, comes from a paper written in 2000 by Roy Fielding, one of the people who wrote HTTP. It describes an API as a set of resources, each with its own URL, and it uses HTTP's methods as the verbs. Clients get and send representations of those resources, here in JSON:

| Request | Means |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/rooms` | list the rooms |
| `GET /v1/rooms/3` | get room 3 |
| `POST /v1/rooms` | add a room to the collection |
| `PUT /v1/rooms/3` | replace room 3 with what's sent |
| `PATCH /v1/rooms/3` | change part of room 3 |
| `DELETE /v1/rooms/3` | remove room 3 |

The path names the thing, and the method says what to do to it. Once a client knows that, it can guess most of an API it has never seen.

## The rules that matter

Fielding's paper sets out **constraints**, rules an API follows to count as REST. Three matter most in practice:

- **Stateless.** Each request carries everything needed to answer it, as the previous lesson showed, so any server can answer any request.
- **Cacheable.** Each response says whether it may be kept and reused, with headers like `Cache-Control` and `ETag`. Browsers, and the servers in between, can then answer repeated GETs without asking your API.
- **A uniform interface.** Every resource works the same way: the same methods, the same status codes, and the same error format. Learn one endpoint and you can guess the rest.

The paper has more rules, like putting links to related resources in every response. Most APIs that call themselves REST skip those, and you'll also hear them called **RESTful**, or just JSON over HTTP. Nobody minds.

## Designing the URLs

- **Plural nouns for collections**, like `/rooms` and `/bookings`, and an id for one item, like `/rooms/3`.
- **Shallow nesting.** `/rooms/3/bookings`, room 3's bookings, reads well. `/buildings/1/rooms/3/bookings/1001` goes too deep: a booking has an id of its own, so it lives at `/bookings/1001`.
- **Actions as sub-resources.** Cancelling a booking has rules of its own, like who may do it and until when, so it's `POST /v1/bookings/1001/cancel`, not a PATCH that sets a status.
- **No verbs otherwise.** Not `/getRoom?id=3`, since GET already says get.
- **Lowercase, with dashes between words**, like the file names in the web course.

## What it's good at, and what it costs

REST is plain HTTP, so any client can call it, from curl to a browser to a program in any language, and caching, logging, and security tools all understand it. That's why public APIs almost always use it.

Its cost shows up on busy screens. Each endpoint returns a fixed shape, so a screen often gets fields it never shows, which is called **over-fetching**. And a screen that needs several resources has to ask for each one, often one after another, since it learns the next id from the last answer. That's **under-fetching**, and the example below shows it.

examples.title: Three requests for one screen
examples.prompt: A booking's page in the phone app shows the booking's times, the room's name, and the building's name. With plain REST, that takes three requests to Roombook, here on port 4000.
examples.code:
curl -s -w "
" http://localhost:4000/v1/bookings/1001
curl -s -w "
" http://localhost:4000/v1/rooms/1
curl -s -w "
" http://localhost:4000/v1/buildings
examples.explanation: The first answer is the booking, and its `roomId` says which room to ask for next. The second is the room, and its `building` says which building. The third is every building, since the screen needs one name from it. That's three round trips, one after another, since each depends on the one before, and on a phone each can take a tenth of a second or more. Out of all those fields, the screen shows four: the two times, Turing, and Main Library. Teams fix this in a few ways: an endpoint that can include related data when asked, a BFF that makes the three calls close to the data and answers once, or GraphQL, in the next part. `-s` keeps curl quiet, and `-w` prints a line break after each answer, since these bodies don't end with one.

steps.title: GraphQL
steps.body:
GraphQL was built at Facebook in 2012 for its phone app, whose screens needed data from many places over slow connections: under-fetching at its worst. It turns the question around. Instead of the server deciding what each endpoint returns, the client says exactly what it wants.

## One endpoint and a typed schema

A GraphQL API has one endpoint, usually `POST /graphql`. The server publishes a **schema**: every type of thing it knows, each field on it, and each field's type. Here's part of a schema for Roombook, in GraphQL's own language:

```text
type Query {
  booking(id: ID!): Booking
}

type Booking {
  id: ID!
  startsAt: String!
  endsAt: String!
  room: Room!
}

type Room {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  capacity: Int!
  building: Building!
}
```

`type Query` lists what clients can ask for at the top, here one booking by its id, and `!` means never null. A field can hold another type, like a booking's `room`, so a client can follow from one thing to the next in a single request. The client sends a **query**, which names the fields it wants and has the same shape as the answer it gets back:

```text
{
  booking(id: 1001) {
    startsAt
    endsAt
    room {
      name
      building {
        name
      }
    }
  }
}
```

```diagram api-styles-fetching
The same screen's data: three round trips with REST, one with GraphQL.
```

## Queries, mutations, and subscriptions

A **query** reads. A **mutation** changes something, like `createBooking`, and names the fields it wants back. A **subscription** keeps a connection open, usually a WebSocket, so the server can push changes as they happen.

On the server, each field has a **resolver**: a function that fetches that field's data. A GraphQL library reads the query, checks it against the schema, calls the resolver for every field asked for, and builds the answer in the query's shape. You write the schema and the resolvers, and the library does the rest.

## The N+1 problem

Resolvers make one trap easy to fall into. Ask for 50 rooms with each room's building, and a simple server runs 1 database query for the rooms, then 1 more for each room's building: 51 queries, or N+1 for N rooms. The usual fix is a **data loader**, which collects every id asked for in one step of the answer and fetches them all with one query. REST code can fall into the same trap, and the database lessons show how to avoid it there.

## What it costs

- **Caching is harder.** Every request is a POST to the same URL, so browsers and the servers in between can't keep copies. Clients keep their own copies instead, by each object's id.
- **Errors come back with 200 OK.** A field that failed shows up in an `errors` list next to the data, as the second example shows, so status codes stop telling you much, and monitoring has to read bodies.
- **Clients can ask for too much.** A query nested ten levels deep can cost the server a fortune, so servers limit how deep and how costly a query may be.
- **More machinery.** Both sides need a GraphQL library, and the schema is one more thing to keep in step.

GraphQL shines when many different clients need different slices of the same data, like one company's web, phone, and TV apps. For one website and one phone app, REST is usually simpler.

examples.title: One query for the whole screen
examples.prompt: Send that query to a GraphQL version of Roombook, on port 4000. The query travels inside a JSON body, as a string, here written on one line.
examples.code: curl -s --json '{"query": "{ booking(id: 1001) { startsAt endsAt room { name building { name } } } }"}' http://localhost:4000/graphql
examples.explanation: The answer has the same shape as the query, inside a top-level `data`: the booking's two times, then the room's name and its building's name, nested the way the query nested them. Nothing else came back, and it took one round trip. Compare it with the three REST answers in the previous part, which sent every field of three resources. The server did the same work, finding the booking, the room, and the building, but it did it next to the data, and sent only what the screen shows.

examples.title: An error, with 200 OK
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking that doesn't exist. `-w` prints the status code after the body, on a line of its own.
examples.explanation: The status code on the last line is 200, even though nothing was found. The failure is in the body: an `errors` list, where each error has a `message`, the `locations` in the query it came from, line 1 and column 3, and the `path` to the field that failed. `data` is still there, with `booking` set to null. That's on purpose: a query can ask for ten fields and have one fail, and the other nine should still arrive. But it means a client, or a dashboard that counts failures, can't trust the status code. It has to look for `errors` in every answer.

steps.title: gRPC
steps.body:
When a company's own services call each other millions of times a minute, JSON's text and HTTP/1.1's one request at a time per connection start to cost real money. gRPC, released by Google in 2015, is built for those calls.

## A contract in a .proto file

A gRPC API is written down first, in a `.proto` file, using **Protocol Buffers**, or **protobuf**: a language for describing messages, where every field has a type and a number. The example below shows Roombook's rooms service in it. A **service** lists the calls, and each call takes one message and returns another.

From that file, a tool called `protoc`, or a newer one called Buf, **generates code** in each language: a **client stub**, an object whose methods make the calls, and a server interface for you to fill in. Calling another service then looks like calling a function. That's where the name comes from: **RPC** stands for remote procedure call, calling a function that runs in another program as if it were in yours. Here's a call in TypeScript, through generated code:

```ts
const room = await client.getRoom({ id: 1n }, { timeoutMs: 2000 });
console.log(room.name);
```

`client` comes from the code generated for Node.js, here with Connect's library. Protobuf's 64-bit numbers become JavaScript's `bigint`, which is why the id is written `1n`, and `timeoutMs` sets the deadline.

## Binary messages over HTTP/2

gRPC messages are binary: each field is sent as its number and its value, with no names and no quotes. They're smaller than JSON and much faster for computers to read and write, though you can't read them yourself. They travel over HTTP/2, which, as the web course showed, lets many requests share one connection at the same time.

```diagram api-styles-grpc
One .proto file generates both sides, which then talk over one HTTP/2 connection.
```

A call can be **unary**, one request and one answer, like `GetRoom`, or it can **stream**. A server stream sends many answers to one request, like `WatchAvailability` sending a message each time a room's free times change. A client stream sends many requests, and both sides can stream at once.

## Deadlines and status codes

Every gRPC call can carry a **deadline**: how long the caller is willing to wait. The deadline travels with the call, so a service that calls three more can pass on what's left of it, and nobody keeps working on an answer nobody is waiting for. gRPC has its own status codes too, like `OK`, `NOT_FOUND`, `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, and `UNAVAILABLE`. They're sent after the message, in a **trailer**, a header that comes at the end. The Distributed Systems section covers deadlines in every style.

## Where it fits

gRPC suits calls between services you own: fast, typed on both sides, and with streaming built in. It's a poor fit for browsers. A page's `fetch` can't read trailers or drive HTTP/2 the way gRPC needs, so a browser needs a bridge: **gRPC-Web**, with a proxy that translates, or **Connect**, a protocol that speaks gRPC between services and plain HTTP with JSON to browsers. It's also harder to poke at, since curl can't read binary, so you need tools like `grpcurl` or Postman. That's why many companies use gRPC on the inside and REST on the outside.

examples.title: Roombook's rooms service in protobuf
examples.prompt: A `.proto` file, `proto/roombook/v1/rooms.proto`, that describes two calls on rooms. Both sides of a gRPC API generate their code from a file like this.
examples.explanation: `syntax = "proto3"` picks the current version of the language, and `package` keeps these names apart from other files' names. The `service` lists two calls. `GetRoom` takes a `GetRoomRequest` and returns a `Room`. `WatchAvailability` returns a `stream` of `Availability` messages, one each time the room's free times change. Each `message` lists fields, each with a type, a name, and a number, and `repeated` means a list. The numbers are what travel on the wire, not the names. So a field can be renamed without breaking anyone, but its number can never be reused for something else. That rule is how gRPC APIs change safely: add fields with new numbers, and old clients skip what they don't know. The generated code turns names like `room_id` into each language's style, like `roomId` or `RoomId`.

steps.title: Real time: polling, SSE, and WebSockets
steps.body:
HTTP has one built-in limit: the client asks and the server answers, and the server never speaks first. But some screens need news the moment it happens, like a door screen that should show a booking as soon as it's made, or a chat message that should appear without a reload. There are four common ways to get it, and they trade simplicity for speed.

```diagram api-styles-realtime
The same news reaches the client four ways. Each dot is news happening on the server.
```

## Short polling

The client asks again every few seconds, like `GET /v1/rooms/1/availability` every 10 seconds. It's plain REST, so it works everywhere, and caches help. But most answers say nothing changed, and news waits for the next ask, up to 10 seconds here. The cost adds up: a thousand door screens asking every 10 seconds is 100 requests a second, all day, for news that comes a few times an hour. In the diagram's first row, each piece of news waits on the server until the next ask.

## Long polling

The client asks, and the server doesn't answer until there's news, or until a time limit like 30 seconds runs out. Then the client asks again at once. News arrives almost straight away, and there are far fewer empty answers. But every waiting client holds a connection open on the server, and the code is fiddly on both sides. Older chat apps were built this way.

## Server-sent events

**Server-sent events**, or **SSE**, which the web course met as `EventSource`, keep one response open and send events down it as they happen. It's still plain HTTP: the client sends one GET, and the server answers with `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and a body that never ends. Each event is a few lines of text, like `event:`, `data:`, and `id:`, with a blank line after it. The example below shows a stream.

It only goes one way, from server to client. That's what most live updates need, and SSE brings two gifts with it. The browser's `EventSource` reconnects by itself if the connection drops, after waiting as long as the server's `retry:` line says. And when it reconnects, it sends the last `id:` it saw in a `Last-Event-ID` header, so the server can send what it missed.

## WebSockets

A **WebSocket**, which the web course met as `new WebSocket(...)`, is a connection where both sides can send at any moment. It starts as an HTTP GET with an `Upgrade: websocket` header, and the server agrees with a `101 Switching Protocols` status:

```http
GET /v1/chat HTTP/1.1
Host: api.roombook.example
Connection: Upgrade
Upgrade: websocket
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Connection: Upgrade
Upgrade: websocket
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=
```

`Sec-WebSocket-Key` is a random value, and `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` is worked out from it, which proves the server really speaks WebSocket. After the 101, the connection stops being HTTP. It carries **frames**, small messages that either side can send at any time, until one side closes it.

WebSockets suit chat, multiplayer games, and documents that many people edit at once, where messages flow both ways all the time. What you give up is what HTTP gave you: there are no status codes, no caching, and no headers on each message, so you design your own messages, and you write the reconnecting yourself.

## Long-lived connections are hard to scale

SSE, long polling, and WebSockets all keep connections open, often for hours. Each one is held by one server process, and that causes two problems once you run more than one. News that happens on one server has to reach the clients connected to the others. And every time you release a new version, every connection drops and has to reconnect. Holding the connections is cheap for Node.js, since an idle connection is only a little memory, waiting on the event loop, the part of Node.js that Your First Express Project explains. The Distributed Systems section solves the first problem with Redis.

examples.title: A stream of events
examples.prompt: Ask Roombook, on port 4000, for room 1's live availability. `-N` makes curl print each piece the moment it arrives, instead of saving it up. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Powered-By: Express
Content-Type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
Cache-Control: no-cache
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:14:07 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

retry: 5000

id: 41
event: availability
data: {"roomId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:30:00Z","available":false}

id: 42
event: availability
data: {"roomId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T16:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T17:00:00Z","available":false}

id: 43
event: availability
data: {"roomId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:30:00Z","available":true}
examples.explanation: The headers came at once, with `text/event-stream` as the content type, and then curl kept waiting, since the body never ends. The `retry` line asks the client to wait five seconds before reconnecting, if the connection ever drops. Then an event arrived each second, each one a few lines and a blank line. `id` numbers the event, so a client that reconnects can say where it got to. `event` names the kind of event, and `data` holds its content, JSON here. Read in order, they say that 14:00 to 15:30 was booked, then 16:00 to 17:00, and then the first booking was cancelled, so that time is free again. A door screen would redraw after each one.

steps.title: Webhooks and other styles
steps.body:
Polling and push channels need the client to keep a connection open. When the client is another company's server, there's a simpler way: when something happens, call it.

## A webhook is your server calling theirs

A **webhook** is a request your server sends to a URL that a customer gave you, whenever an event they care about happens. Say a calendar app wants to know about bookings. It registers `https://calendar.example/hooks/roombook` with Roombook, once. From then on, each time a booking is confirmed, Roombook sends a POST to that URL. The roles flip: Roombook is now the client, and the calendar app is the server. Stripe tells shops about payments this way, and GitHub tells build servers about new code.

```diagram api-styles-webhook
A delivery fails, waits, and goes out again until the receiver answers 2xx.
```

## What a delivery holds

Here's one delivery from Roombook:

```http
POST /hooks/roombook HTTP/1.1
Host: calendar.example
Content-Type: application/json
Roombook-Signature: t=1790845200,v1=8103f81aedb43b381cea3882c08c71a39f02147b87c1d17379ab75f9f9f57118

{"id":"evt_3f2a91c4","type":"booking.confirmed","createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z","data":{"id":1001,"roomId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:30:00Z"}}
```

The body carries an **event id**, unique to this event, a **type** that says what happened, when it happened, and the **payload**, the data about it. The `Roombook-Signature` header proves the delivery came from Roombook. When the customer registered, Roombook gave them a secret, and it signs every delivery with it: an **HMAC**, a code computed from the secret, the timestamp `t`, and the body. Anyone could find or guess the URL, but only someone with the secret can make a matching signature.

## Rules for receivers

- **Verify the signature** before trusting anything in the body, and reject the delivery if its timestamp is more than a few minutes old, so someone who copied an old one can't send it again.
- **Answer fast.** Reply 2xx within a few seconds, and do the real work afterwards. The sender gives up on slow answers and tries again.
- **Expect duplicates.** If your 200 got lost on its way back, the sender can't tell, so it sends the event again. Keep the ids of the events you've handled, and skip repeats.
- **Don't rely on order.** A retry can arrive after a later event.

Senders have rules too: retry with longer and longer waits, for hours or days, and keep a log of every delivery, so customers can see what was sent. The Distributed Systems section builds both sides, and the Production section shows why a URL that customers choose is a security risk.

## Other styles you'll hear about

- **SOAP** is an older style that sends XML, with a formal contract file. Banks, governments, and older business systems still use it.
- **JSON-RPC** posts a JSON object that names a method and its arguments, like `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getRoom","params":{"id":1},"id":7}`. It's simple, and it's what MCP, the protocol AI assistants use to call tools, is built on.
- **tRPC** lets a TypeScript client call TypeScript functions on the server directly, with their types shared and no schema to write. It's a good fit when one team writes both sides in TypeScript, as an Express team can.
- **Message brokers**, like RabbitMQ and Kafka, carry messages between services through a middleman: one service drops a message off, and another picks it up later, even if the first has stopped. It isn't request and response at all, and the Distributed Systems section covers it.

steps.title: Choosing a style
steps.body:
Most systems use more than one style. The question is never which style is best, but which one fits each job.

## The styles side by side

| Style | Who speaks | What travels | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| REST | the client asks, the server answers | JSON over HTTP | public APIs, web and phone backends | over-fetching and under-fetching |
| GraphQL | the client asks, the server answers | a query, and JSON in its shape | many clients that need different data | caching, query limits, errors with 200 |
| gRPC | either side calls or streams | binary protobuf over HTTP/2 | calls between your own services | browsers need a bridge |
| Polling | the client asks again and again | JSON over HTTP | rare news, simple clients | wasted requests, late news |
| SSE | the server pushes | text events over HTTP | live updates to clients | one way only |
| WebSockets | both sides, any time | frames | chat, games, editing together | scaling, and messages you design |
| Webhooks | your server calls theirs | JSON over HTTP | telling other systems about events | signatures, retries, duplicates |

## Rules of thumb

- **A public API: REST.** Everyone can call it with any tool, and HTTP caching works.
- **Calls between your own services, at high volume: gRPC.**
- **Many clients with very different screens: GraphQL**, often as a layer in front of REST or gRPC services.
- **Updates from server to client: SSE first.** Reach for WebSockets only when the client also sends a steady stream of messages.
- **Telling another company's system that something happened: webhooks.**

## What Roombook uses

Roombook uses three styles:

- **REST** for everything its clients ask for, from the Handling Requests section on.
- **SSE** for each room's live availability, which the door screens and the website listen to, in the Distributed Systems section.
- **Webhooks** for booking events sent to calendar apps, in the same section.

It skips GraphQL, since its screens are simple and its clients are few. It skips gRPC, since it's one service, with no other services of its own to call. And it skips WebSockets, since its clients only listen.

## Each style in Express

| Style | In Express |
|---|---|
| REST | Express itself |
| GraphQL | Apollo Server, or GraphQL Yoga |
| gRPC | `@grpc/grpc-js`, or Connect for Node.js |
| SSE | Express itself, writing to the response |
| WebSockets | `ws`, or Socket.IO |
| Webhooks | `fetch` to send, and `express.raw()` to receive |
| tRPC | tRPC, with its Express adapter |

You won't need most of these in this course, but each style is only a package away. On the receiving side of a webhook, read the body as raw bytes, since the signature was computed over exactly the bytes that were sent.

That's the outside of APIs. The next lesson, Your First Express Project, starts building Roombook's REST API.

recap:
- REST models an API as resources with URLs, uses HTTP's methods as verbs, and gets HTTP caching for free.
- REST's fixed shapes can send too much, or need several round trips for one screen.
- GraphQL has one endpoint and a typed schema, and the client picks its fields, at the cost of HTTP caching and status codes.
- gRPC sends binary protobuf messages over HTTP/2, with generated code and deadlines, and suits calls between services.
- Polling asks again and again, SSE streams events from the server, and WebSockets carry messages both ways after a 101.
- A webhook is your server calling a URL the customer registered: signed, retried, and safe to receive twice.
- Roombook uses REST, SSE for live availability, and webhooks for booking events.
